hints: Focus on how many C=C double bonds limonene has and what excess HCl means for how many of them will react.
Recall Markovnikov's rule for dry HCl, the H adds to the carbon with more H atoms already so the Cl ends up on the more substituted, more stable carbocation position.
Apply that rule to both double bonds in limonene, the trisubstituted ring alkene and the terminal side-chain alkene, to place both Cl atoms on tertiary carbons.
walkthrough:
**Spot the two alkenes**

Limonene has two separate C=C bonds. One is inside the six-membered ring and one is in the side chain outside the ring.

With excess dry $HCl$, both alkenes will undergo electrophilic addition:
$$C=C + HCl \rightarrow CH-CCl$$

**Remember Markovnikov addition**

For $HCl$, the $H^+$ adds first to make the most stable carbocation. In practice, H goes to the carbon that already has more H atoms, and Cl goes to the more substituted carbon.

Tertiary carbocations are more stable than secondary, which are more stable than primary.

**Add HCl to the ring double bond**

The ring $C=C$ is trisubstituted. Adding $H^+$ to the $CH$ end gives a tertiary carbocation on the carbon bearing the methyl group.

So $Cl$ ends up on that top tertiary carbon to give $C(CH_3)Cl$ in the ring.

**Add HCl to the side-chain double bond**

The side chain $C=C(CH_3)_2$ is terminal, $C(CH_3)=CH_2$. Adding $H^+$ to the $CH_2$ end gives a tertiary carbocation on the $(CH_3)_2C^+$ carbon.

So $Cl$ ends up there to give $C(CH_3)_2Cl$. Both additions are Markovnikov, giving two tertiary chlorides.

options.A: This shows correct Markovnikov addition to the ring alkene only. It is incomplete because excess HCl will also add to the side-chain alkene, so a dichloride is needed.
options.B: This shows only one HCl added and the Cl is on the less substituted ring carbon. That is anti-Markovnikov addition via a less stable secondary carbocation, so it will not be the major product.
options.C: This shows two Markovnikov additions. Cl is on the tertiary carbon in the ring and on the tertiary carbon in the side chain, both via the most stable tertiary carbocations. This matches excess HCl addition to both double bonds.
options.D: This shows addition to both double bonds but both Cl atoms are on the less substituted carbons. That is anti-Markovnikov addition at both sites and would go via less stable carbocations, so it is not major.
